messages.subject: wiener_rng in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Dear HBayesDM Team,

We are fitting Drift Diffusion Models in Stan and we are interested in running a few posterior predictive checks.
Based on your package (choiceRT_ddm_single.stan file) and on various Stan forums,  wiener_rng function is not yet officially introduced to Stan.
Did you try by any chance implementing this function in Stan? If not, do you have a suggestion what could be a reliable alternative?

Thanks! And thanks for the great package.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: wiener_rng in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

Thanks for your interest!

While we have not implemented an rng function within Stan, I have experimented with the following R package that can be used to take draws from a wiener process: https://rdrr.io/cran/RWiener/man/wienerdist.html

Actually, I used this package to help ensure that our Stan code was working properly by doing a small parameter recovery study and it worked quite well. I have attached that R script here.

What you would need to do is use the rwiener() function from the package noted above to simulate random draw from each posterior sample and for each subject. This can all be done in R, similar to how the parameter recovery code is doing simulations.

Anyway, I hope this helps!

Best,
Nate

Thanks a lot

Best,
Suiqing

messages.subject: Warning messages and model fit
messages.body_plain:
Dear hBayesDM team,

Thank you for maintaining this package.  I have a couple questions about warning messages and inferences.

One general question regards the pareto k warning message.  Is there any time when action should be taken based on the warning?

A more specific question regards drawing inferences about model fit for two groups.  Here are the details:

The ORL model was conducted with data from two groups, each n = 59.
For the first group, there were no warning messages.  For the second group, there were multiple warnings (see code and details below).

Warnings #1-2 were the same.
[1: In UseMethod("depth") :no applicable method for 'depth' applied to an object of class "NULL"]

- Is there a reference to this warning somewhere?

Warnings #3-4 were about low ESS.  I plan to increase the iters in an attempt to have reliable posteriors.
- Should I also infer that model fits group 1 better than group 2 based on the "low ESS"?

If I was going to test that question statistically, I would probably:
1. run model for group 2 with 10k iters and see if errors are resolved.
2a (if errors are resolved): run model for group 1 with 10k iters and compare LOOIC between identical models for each group.
2b (if errors are not resolved): adjust model specifications and make sure errors are resolved before comparing the LOOIC.

Sum:
- If a model results in low ESS for a group, does fit that sample less well than a sample which did not result in a low ESS warning?
- To make inferences based on LOOIC, try to compare identical models that did not result in warning messages to assess model fit between groups.

Any details about where and how this logic is flawed would be appreciated.  I don't have permission to share the data, but the details are attached.

Thanks,
Paul

messages.subject: Re: Warning messages and model fit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

Thanks for your interest!

Regarding your questions:

1) Pareto k's: We often get these messages due to the way that hBayesDM sums like log likelihood across trials within subjects before computing the LOOIC metrics. After doing the sum, the pareto k estimates tend to be high. In all the models I have tested without the summation, the pareto k's are low, but the results of the model comparison have been the same (both methods give the same answer). Still, this is not ideal and it is something we should probably think about in the future (e.g., just returning the subject by trial log-likelihoods as opposed to summing across trials). If you would like to, you could modify the Stan code to not do the summation and see if your inference changes (to do this, you can use syntax similar to the posterior predictions in the `generated quantities` block).

2) For this warning message: "In UseMethod("depth") :no applicable method for 'depth' applied to an object of class "NULL"", it may be related to convergence issues, but I am not totally sure. I saw this post on the Stan discord, which suggests it could be convergence: https://discourse.mc-stan.org/t/problem-running-mixed-effect-model-with-ordinal-outcome-and-ordinal-predictors-with-brms/8213/2

3) For "Should I also infer that model fits group 1 better than group 2 based on the "low ESS"?
", I would advise against this, because it is a problem with parameter estimation rather than model fit per se. It is true that you could be having convergence problem because the model is poor for the data (which seems to be what you are getting at?), but it is just as likely that you could improve ESS with some changes to the tuning parameters, etc. I would first check your raw data to make sure things look OK, and then go for more iterations, try a different random seed, and increase adapt_delta to .9 or so to see if it makes a difference. You could also try setting different initial parameter values if your chains are getting stuck, which can cause low ESS.

4) For "

- If a model results in low ESS for a group, does fit that sample less well than a sample which did not result in a low ESS warning?
- To make inferences based on LOOIC, try to compare identical models that did not result in warning messages to assess model fit between groups."

As alluded to above (response to 3), you would want to go for the second point. Only after the models have converged and you have a decent ESS can you really interpret any of these metrics.

On a final note, you should not need 10k + samples per chain. When modifying adapt_delta and other tuning parameters, this could make it take quite a while to run. I find it helpful to start with ~ 1000 samples per chain (with ~ 200-300 warmup) while debegging things like this, and then once it looks like chains are converging well I might collect ~3000-4000 samples per chain with ~1000 warmup samples (across ~4 chains). This way, you will not have to wait all day for a model that fails to converge.

It would also be helpful to see traceplots of the chains if you can attach them here, as well as a pairs plot of the parameter estimates (e.g., `pairs(my_fit, pars = c("mu_Arew", "mu_Apun", "mu_k", "mu_betaF", "mu_betaP", "sigma"))`)

Best,
Nate

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nate,

Thanks for the quick reply and the clear info!

1) If you've already tested the Stan modification without noticing any change in the models, it's probably safe to disregard the warning.

2) I wasn't sure how to tackle the "In UseMethod("depth") :no applicable method for 'depth' applied to an object of class "NULL" warning, so I ran the exact same model again and it didn't replicate.

3-4) Glad to confirm that warning messages do not equal poor fit.  When using the LOOIC to compare model fit for two groups, is it important to run each model with exactly the same specifications?  In other words, would it be more appropriate to compare LOOIC for:

group1: ORL model with 2k iters and no adjustment
  to
group2: ORL model with 4k iters and adapt_delta=0.99

OR

group1: ORL model with 4k iters and adapt_delta=0.99
  to
group2: ORL model with 4k iters and adapt_delta=0.99

I attached trace plots from each of the troubleshooting steps and a pairs plot of the parameter estimates for group 2 for the final model.

Please let me know if you notice anything unusual, or more info would be helpful.

Thanks,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

Of course!

Regarding your question:

"3-4) Glad to confirm that warning messages do not equal poor fit.  When using the LOOIC to compare model fit for two groups, is it important to run each model with exactly the same specifications?  In other words, would it be more appropriate to compare LOOIC for:

group1: ORL model with 2k iters and no adjustment
  to
group2: ORL model with 4k iters and adapt_delta=0.99

OR

group1: ORL model with 4k iters and adapt_delta=0.99
  to
group2: ORL model with 4k iters and adapt_delta=0.99"

As long as your chains are well mixed and you are confident that you have reached convergence to the target posteriors (and have enough samples to make inference), you can compare models with different numbers of samples. I generally do try to use models with the same number of samples, but it is not strictly necessary—especially if your models are taking a long time to fit.

Best,
Nate

On Monday, April 27, 2020 at 10:15:21 AM UTC-4, Haines, Nathaniel B. wrote:
> Hi Paul,
>
> Thanks for your interest!
>
> Regarding your questions:
>
> 1) Pareto k's: We often get these messages due to the way that hBayesDM sums like log likelihood across trials within subjects before computing the LOOIC metrics. After doing the sum, the pareto k estimates tend to be high. In all the models I have tested without the summation, the pareto k's are low, but the results of the model comparison have been the same (both methods give the same answer). Still, this is not ideal and it is something we should probably think about in the future (e.g., just returning the subject by trial log-likelihoods as opposed to summing across trials). If you would like to, you could modify the Stan code to not do the summation and see if your inference changes (to do this, you can use syntax similar to the posterior predictions in the `generated quantities` block).
>
> 2) For this warning message: "In UseMethod("depth") :no applicable method for 'depth' applied to an object of class "NULL"", it may be related to convergence issues, but I am not totally sure. I saw this post on the Stan discord, which suggests it could be convergence: https://discourse.mc-stan.org/t/problem-running-mixed-effect-model-with-ordinal-outcome-and-ordinal-predictors-with-brms/8213/2 <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://discourse.mc-stan.org/t/problem-running-mixed-effect-model-with-ordinal-outcome-and-ordinal-predictors-with-brms/8213/2__;!!KGKeukY!g195NsDPX6z6z9aHngLgpc5nOIQFBfL1pPJaVViV1FCEZMqO9LDkzkKGvHSx4lIamcR3aIwPb_7i$>
>
> 3) For "Should I also infer that model fits group 1 better than group 2 based on the "low ESS"?
> ", I would advise against this, because it is a problem with parameter estimation rather than model fit per se. It is true that you could be having convergence problem because the model is poor for the data (which seems to be what you are getting at?), but it is just as likely that you could improve ESS with some changes to the tuning parameters, etc. I would first check your raw data to make sure things look OK, and then go for more iterations, try a different random seed, and increase adapt_delta to .9 or so to see if it makes a difference. You could also try setting different initial parameter values if your chains are getting stuck, which can cause low ESS.
>
> 4) For "
> - If a model results in low ESS for a group, does fit that sample less well than a sample which did not result in a low ESS warning?
> - To make inferences based on LOOIC, try to compare identical models that did not result in warning messages to assess model fit between groups."
>
> As alluded to above (response to 3), you would want to go for the second point. Only after the models have converged and you have a decent ESS can you really interpret any of these metrics.
>
> On a final note, you should not need 10k + samples per chain. When modifying adapt_delta and other tuning parameters, this could make it take quite a while to run. I find it helpful to start with ~ 1000 samples per chain (with ~ 200-300 warmup) while debegging things like this, and then once it looks like chains are converging well I might collect ~3000-4000 samples per chain with ~1000 warmup samples (across ~4 chains). This way, you will not have to wait all day for a model that fails to converge.
>
> It would also be helpful to see traceplots of the chains if you can attach them here, as well as a pairs plot of the parameter estimates (e.g., `pairs(my_fit, pars = c("mu_Arew", "mu_Apun", "mu_k", "mu_betaF", "mu_betaP", "sigma"))`)
>
> Best,
> Nate
